q: Is the SEC climate disclosure rule in force, and do US buyers still need my emissions?
title: SEC climate rule status and US buyers
short: No. The SEC adopted its climate disclosure rules in March 2024, stayed them in April 2024, and in March 2025 voted to stop defending them in court, so they have never taken effect. US buyers still ask for supplier emissions because of their own targets, CDP, California's SB 253 and EU rules.
audience: Indian exporters to US companies; Indian companies with US listings

sections.h: What happened to the SEC rules
ul: 6 March 2024: the SEC adopted rules (Release No. 33-11275) requiring listed companies to disclose climate risks and, for larger filers, material Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions.
4 April 2024: the SEC stayed the rules while legal challenges, consolidated in the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, were heard.
27 March 2025: the SEC voted to end its defence of the rules. The court then held the case in abeyance, waiting for the SEC to decide whether to withdraw or change them.
The rules never reached their first compliance date.

sections.h: Even in force, the rules asked nothing of suppliers
p: The final SEC rules dropped Scope 3. They covered a listed company's own Scope 1 and Scope 2, and only for large accelerated and accelerated filers where material. An Indian supplier was never in scope. An Indian company with a US listing that files with the SEC would have been, which is why those companies should watch the docket.

sections.h: Why US buyers still send data requests
ul: Their own climate targets, many validated by SBTi, which include supplier emissions in Scope 3.
CDP supply chain programmes, run on behalf of large buyers each year.
California's SB 253, which requires US companies above USD 1 billion in revenue doing business in California to report Scope 3 from 2027.
EU subsidiaries of US groups that report under the CSRD.

sections.h: What to send a US buyer
p: A full year of Scope 1 and location-based Scope 2 in tonnes, built on the GHG Protocol, with each factor and its source, plus market-based Scope 2 if you hold certificates or green power contracts. Add your output or revenue for the same year so the buyer can allocate a share, and say which figures come from bills and which are estimates.

senseible: Senseible prepares Scope 1 and Scope 2 from your invoices and electricity bills, with the factor and source on every line, as a self-declared data pack you can send to a buyer. It does not track SEC litigation or fill in a buyer's portal for you.
